summary.name: How Google Backs Up the Internet
summary.one_liner: A High Scalability write-up of Google SRE Raymond Blum's talk on how Google backs up exabytes of data, covering restore-focused design, tape redundancy, and automation.
use_cases: Designing backup systems that scale to very large data volumes
Learning how to verify backups with continuous restore tests
Planning disaster recovery testing and site redundancy
Understanding tape-based backup with parity across tapes
Studying how to automate operations to avoid linear staffing growth
summary.what_it_does: The page summarizes a talk by Google SRE Raymond Blum on how Google backs up its data at exabyte scale. The main theme is that restores matter more than backups, so the system is designed to make restores fast and simple while backups can be complex. It describes writing data to tape with parity across tapes (4 data tapes plus 1 XOR code tape), running continuous restore tests on random samples of backups, and checksum-based comparisons. It also covers automation of scheduling, tape failure handling, and machine failure handling so humans are not involved in steady-state operations. The GMail 2011 outage is discussed as a case study in recovering data from overlapping layers of the stack.
notable: Restore-first design: backups are treated as a tax paid for fast, simple restores
RAID-like parity across tapes (4 data tapes plus 1 XOR tape) with continuous restore sampling
Explicit rule that scaling effort must not be linear with data growth, enforced by automation
GMail 2011 outage recovery explained as overlap across tape, replication, front-ends and logs
caveats: Secondhand summary of a talk; Google did not disclose its total data size or many implementation details
Some details, such as the encryption-key deletion approach, were not explained by the speaker
Describes Google systems as of 2014 (GFS replaced around a year before by Colossus)
